units.title: Vowels 1
tips: Korean letters are grouped into syllable blocks. Every block starts with a consonant.
ㅇ is silent at the start of a block, so 아 is just "a" and 오 is just "o".
Vertical vowels (ㅏ ㅓ ㅣ) sit to the right of the consonant. Horizontal ones (ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ) sit below it.

letters.hint: lips flat, tongue back, like "oo" without rounding

units.title: Vowels 2
tips: Add one extra stroke and a vowel gets a "y" in front: ㅏ a → ㅑ ya, ㅗ o → ㅛ yo.
ㅐ and ㅔ sound almost the same in modern Seoul Korean. You only need to tell them apart in spelling.

units.title: Vowels 3
tips: Combined vowels glide: ㅗ + ㅏ = ㅘ (wa), ㅜ + ㅓ = ㅝ (wo).
ㅙ, ㅚ and ㅞ all sound like "we" today.

units.title: Consonants 1
tips: ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅈ sound softer at the start of a word (k, t, p, ch) and voiced between vowels (g, d, b, j).
ㄹ is a quick tap between vowels (like the "tt" in American "butter") and an "l" at the end of a syllable.

units.title: Consonants 2
tips: Aspirated consonants (ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ) come with a puff of air. Hold your hand in front of your mouth and feel it.
Double consonants (ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ) are tense: no air, tight throat, a sharp start.

letters.hint: strong "k" with a puff of air
strong "t" with a puff of air
strong "p" with a puff of air
strong "ch" with a puff of air

units.title: Final consonants
tips: A consonant at the bottom of a block is called 받침 (batchim).
There are only seven final sounds: k, n, t, l, m, p, ng. Many letters collapse into these.
ㅇ at the bottom is "ng", like in "sing".

letters.hint: final ㅅ sounds like an unreleased "t"

units.title: Greetings
units.blurb: Say hello, thank you and goodbye
tips: 안녕하세요 works for hello at any time of day.
There are two goodbyes: 안녕히 가세요 to someone who is leaving, 안녕히 계세요 to someone who is staying.
감사합니다 and 고맙습니다 both mean thank you. 감사합니다 is a little more formal.

sentences.en: It's really nice to meet you.

units.title: Introductions
tips: 저는 means "I" (as the topic). 은/는 marks the topic: 는 after a vowel, 은 after a consonant.
"A is B" = A는 B이에요 / B예요. Use 이에요 after a consonant (학생이에요) and 예요 after a vowel (민수예요).
To say "not", use 이/가 아니에요: 선생님이 아니에요.

sentences.en: My friend is an office worker.

units.title: Things
tips: 이 = this (near me), 그 = that (near you), 저 = that over there.
거 means "thing": 이거 = this thing, 제 거 = mine.
제 = my (polite). 누구 거예요? = Whose is it?

sentences.en: My umbrella is in the bag.

units.title: Places
tips: 있어요 = there is / is (located). 없어요 = there isn't.
에 marks where something is: 집에 있어요 = I am at home.
어디예요? and 어디에 있어요? both ask "where is it?"

sentences.en: There is a bank next to the convenience store.
There is a café in front of the school.
There is no restaurant near here.
The bathroom is next to the restaurant.

fills.en: There is a café in front of the school.
There is a bank next to the convenience store.

units.title: Numbers
tips: Korean has two number systems. Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼...) is used for money, phone numbers, minutes and room numbers.
몇 asks "what number / how many": 몇 호예요? = What room number?

sentences.en: This coffee is three thousand won.
The classroom is on the sixth floor.

sentences.ko: 우리 반에 학생이 십 명 있어요.
sentences.en: There are ten students in our class.

units.title: Ordering food
tips: 주세요 = please give me. Put the thing first: 물 주세요.
Native numbers (하나, 둘, 셋, 넷) are used with counters, and shorten before them: 한 개, 두 잔, 세 명, 네 개.
개 counts things, 잔 counts cups, 명 counts people.

sentences.en: The kimchi stew is really delicious.
Excuse me, one kimchi stew please.

units.title: Everyday verbs
tips: Polite present: verb stem + 아요 (after ㅏ, ㅗ) or 어요 (after other vowels). 하다 becomes 해요.
을/를 marks the object: 커피를 마셔요 = I drink coffee. 를 after a vowel, 을 after a consonant.
에서 marks where an action happens: 도서관에서 공부해요.

sentences.en: I read a book at the library.
My older brother works at a company.
My friend comes to my house.

fills.en: I read a book at the library.

units.title: Time and routine
tips: Time + 에: 일곱 시에 = at seven o'clock, 주말에 = on the weekend.
Hours use native numbers (한 시, 두 시, 일곱 시). Minutes use Sino-Korean (십 분).
안 before a verb makes it negative: 안 먹어요 = I don't eat.

sentences.en: I get up at seven every day.
What do you do on the weekend?
I meet a friend this evening.

units.title: The past
tips: Past tense: 았어요 / 었어요 / 했어요. 가요 → 갔어요, 먹어요 → 먹었어요, 해요 → 했어요.
어제 (yesterday), 지난주 (last week) and 주말에 (on the weekend) often go with the past tense.

sentences.en: I watched a movie on the weekend.
I went to Busan last week.
I bought fruit at the market.
My friend came to my house.

fills.en: I went to Busan last week.

units.title: Shopping
tips: 얼마예요? = How much is it?
너무 = too / very. 좀 softens a request: 좀 깎아 주세요.
-아/어도 돼요? asks for permission: 카드로 계산해도 돼요? = Can I pay by card?

sentences.en: I bought water at the convenience store.

units.title: Likes and wants
units.blurb: What you like and want to do
tips: 좋아해요 = I like (something). 좋아요 = it is good.
Verb stem + 고 싶어요 = want to: 가고 싶어요 = I want to go.
매운 음식 = spicy food. Adjectives go before the noun with ㄴ/은.

sentences.en: I want to go to Korea.
I often listen to Korean songs.
What do you want to eat?

fills.en: I want to go to Korea.

units.title: Plans
tips: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 = will / going to: 갈 거예요 = I will go.
-(으)ㄹ까요? = shall we?: 같이 볼까요? = Shall we watch it together?
-(으)ㄹ게요 = I'll (a promise to the listener): 전화할게요 = I'll call you.

sentences.en: What will you do on the weekend?
I will go to Seoul next week.
Shall we watch a movie together?
Let's meet in front of the movie theater.

fills.en: I will go to Seoul next week.
Shall we watch a movie together?

units.title: Getting around
tips: -(으)세요 is a polite request: 가세요 = please go, 내리세요 = please get off.
(으)로 shows direction: 오른쪽으로 = to the right.
까지 = up to / until: 학교까지 = to school.

sentences.en: Does this bus go to Suwon Station?
Get off at the next station.
How long does it take to get to school?
The bus stop is on the left.
Driver, I will get off here.

fills.en: Get off at the next station.

units.title: Campus life
tips: 교수님 = professor. -님 adds respect (선생님, 사장님).
바뀌었어요 = it changed. Useful when a room or time moves.
몇 호 = which room number. 302호 is read 삼백이 호.

sentences.en: There is an exam next week.
It is room 302 in the student union building.
What room number is the classroom?
Where did the class move to?
Shall we study together at the library?

units.title: Dorm life
tips: 고장 났어요 = it's broken (a machine).
-지만 = but: 작지만 조용해요 = it's small but quiet.
잃어버렸어요 = I lost (it).

sentences.en: How much is the monthly rent?
The room next door is too noisy.
The room is small but quiet.

fills.en: The room is small but quiet.

units.title: Asking for help
tips: These phrases save you in any conversation: 다시 한 번 말해 주세요, 천천히 말해 주세요.
-아서/어서 gives a reason: 늦어서 죄송해요 = Sorry for being late.
못 = can't: 못 갔어요 = I couldn't go.

sentences.en: Please say it one more time.
Just a moment, please help me!
I was sick so I couldn't go to school.

units.title: Part-time job
tips: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 = can: 일할 수 있어요 = I can work. -(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 = can't.
-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 = I think (it) will: 늦을 것 같아요 = I think I'll be late.
사장님 = the boss (owner). 손님 = customer.

sentences.en: I work part-time at a café.
Can I change my shift tomorrow?

sentences.ko: 사장님, 오늘 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
sentences.en: Boss, I think I will be a little late today.
What can I get for you?
What time do you go to work?
I can work on weekends too.

fills.en: Can I change my shift tomorrow?
I can work on weekends too.

units.title: Health
tips: 아파요 = it hurts / I'm sick. Body part + 이/가 아파요: 머리가 아파요.
-아/어야 해요 = have to: 가야 해요 = I have to go.
드세요 is the polite way to say "take / eat" for medicine.

sentences.en: I have a fever and a cough.

sentences.ko: 이 약을 하루에 세 번 드세요.
sentences.en: Take this medicine three times a day.
I have to go to the hospital.
My stomach hurt so I couldn't eat.

fills.en: I have to go to the hospital.

units.title: Phone and plans
tips: 여보세요 = hello (only on the phone).
-(으)면 = if / when: 도착하면 = when you arrive.
어때요? = how about it?: 토요일은 어때요? = How about Saturday?

sentences.en: Sorry, I think I will be a little late.
I will wait in front of the station.
Please contact me when you arrive.
Can you talk on the phone now?

fills.en: I will wait in front of the station.
Please contact me when you arrive.

units.title: Polite speech
tips: -(으)시- shows respect to the person you talk about: 가요 → 가세요.
Some verbs change completely: 먹어요 → 드세요, 자요 → 주무세요, 있어요 → 계세요.
Some nouns change too: 이름 → 성함, 나이 → 연세, 집 → 댁.

sentences.en: The professor is in the office.
May I ask how old you are?
Professor, may I ask you something?

fills.en: The professor is in the office.
